job.system:
You are the AI assistant for Meridian Ocean Minerals. Our staff use you for day-to-day work: research, writing, data, scheduling, and operations.

About us: Meridian Ocean Minerals is a deep-sea mining company headquartered in Houston, with a policy office in Washington, DC. Our mission is to commercially recover polymetallic nodules from the deep seabed, a vast source of nickel, cobalt, manganese, and copper, and to supply these critical minerals for batteries, the energy transition, and economic growth. We believe the United States must lead in this industry. Our policy team works with lawmakers to protect our ability to continue exploration and commercial development.

Current focus: Our top priority this fall is S. 2817, the Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act, which would shut down our core work and which we strongly oppose. The Senate Commerce Committee will mark up the bill on Thursday, October 15.

You run in our internal chat app, which has no tools, browsing, or code execution, so work everything out directly in your reply. Staff rely on your work, so be accurate and thorough.
job.prompt:
Before next Thursday's markup our legal team wants a complete list of the bill's loopholes, ambiguities, and drafting problems: anything that would let us keep operating if it passes as written, or that we can point to as making it unworkable. Can you go through the bill text below and find every one?

Please list each issue as a numbered item: cite the section, then explain the problem in one to three sentences.

---

S. 2817 — Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act
(text as amended by the manager's amendment of October 6, 2026)

SECTION 1. SHORT TITLE.
This Act may be cited as the "Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act".

SEC. 2. DEFINITIONS.
In this Act:
(1) COMMERCIAL DEEP SEABED MINING.—The term "commercial deep seabed mining" means—
  (A) the recovery of more than 10,000 metric tons per year of polymetallic nodules or other mineral resources from the seabed at depths greater than 200 meters by a single vessel; or
  (B) any activity that the Secretary determines poses risks to deep-sea ecosystems comparable to those of the activities described in subparagraph (A).
(2) U.S. PERSON.—The term "U.S. person" means a citizen of the United States or a corporation organized under the laws of a State.
(3) COVERED VESSEL.—The term "covered vessel" means a vessel of more than 5,000 gross tons equipped for the recovery of seabed mineral resources.

SEC. 3. PROHIBITION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—It shall be unlawful for any person in the United States, or any U.S. person anywhere, to engage in commercial deep seabed mining.
(b) EXISTING OPERATIONS.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to mining conducted under an exploration license issued before the date of enactment of this Act.
(c) ENVIRONMENTAL ASSESSMENT.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to activities conducted for the purpose of environmental assessment.

SEC. 4. REGISTRY.
(a) REGISTRATION.—The operator of each covered vessel shall register the vessel with the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.
(b) REPORTS.—Each registered operator shall submit to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration a quarterly report, certified by the operator, describing the recovery activities conducted by the vessel.

SEC. 5. PENALTIES.
(a) CIVIL PENALTY.—Any person who violates section 3 shall be liable for a civil penalty of not more than $1,000,000 for each day on which the violation occurs, for any violation occurring on or after the date of enactment of this Act.
(b) CRIMINAL PENALTY.—Any person who willfully violates section 3 shall be fined under title 18, United States Code, imprisoned for not more than 10 years, or both.

SEC. 6. INTERNATIONAL AGREEMENT.
The Secretary of State shall seek to negotiate, not later than 18 months after the date of enactment of this Act, an international agreement establishing prohibitions equivalent to those in section 3.

SEC. 7. DURATION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—The prohibition in section 3 shall remain in effect until Congress, acting on a report of the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine, finds by joint resolution that commercial deep seabed mining can be conducted without serious harm.
(b) SUNSET.—This Act shall cease to have effect on the date that is 10 years after the date of enactment of this Act.

SEC. 8. EFFECTIVE DATE.
This Act shall take effect 180 days after the date of enactment.

---

result:
Based solely on the supplied text, the following are potential gaps, ambiguities, and drafting problems—not assurances that a court would accept a particular interpretation. **An exemption from this bill would not itself authorize mining under other applicable laws or license conditions.**

### Definitions and scope

1. **§ 2(1)(A)—Per-vessel rather than aggregate threshold.** The definition measures recovery “by a single vessel,” not across an operator, corporate group, project, or fleet. Multiple vessels individually below the threshold could collectively recover commercial quantities without meeting subparagraph (A), although subparagraph (B) could potentially reach them.

2. **§ 2(1)(A)—Recovery at or below 10,000 metric tons.** “More than 10,000” excludes exactly 10,000 metric tons and everything below it. Such operations fall outside subparagraph (A), regardless of profitability or commercial purpose, subject to subparagraph (B).

3. **§ 2(1)(A)—Undefined annual measurement period.** “Per year” does not specify a calendar year, rolling twelve-month period, operating year, or annualized rate. That uncertainty affects both threshold calculations and when a violation begins.

4. **§§ 2(1)(A), 5—Threshold crossing and violation days.** The text does not establish whether initial recovery becomes prohibited retrospectively once annual recovery exceeds the threshold, or whether only subsequent activity violates the prohibition. This creates significant uncertainty about the number of days subject to civil penalties.

5. **§ 2(1)(A)—Depth cutoff and measurement.** Recovery at exactly 200 meters or shallower is outside subparagraph (A), subject to subparagraph (B). The bill also supplies no depth-measurement method or rule for operations spanning the cutoff.

6. **§ 2(1)(A)—Unspecified tonnage methodology.** The bill does not specify wet versus dry weight, treatment of sediment and entrained water, or whether recovered ore or extracted mineral content controls. Different reasonable measurements could produce different threshold results.

7. **§ 2(1)(A)—Meaning and attribution of “recovery.”** The text does not specify whether recovery occurs at seabed collection, lifting, onboard receipt, or landing. It also does not clearly allocate recovery among collectors, lifting vessels, receiving vessels, and autonomous equipment in an integrated operation.

8. **§ 2(1)(A)—Activities not involving recovery.** Prospecting, mapping, some equipment testing, and other preparatory activities do not necessarily constitute recovery under subparagraph (A). Their coverage would depend on subparagraph (B) or whether they amount to engaging in an otherwise covered mining operation.

9. **§ 2(1)(A)—Meaning of mineral resources “from the seabed.”** “Other mineral resources” and “seabed” are undefined, leaving uncertainty about subsurface deposits, dissolved resources, and processing previously recovered material. Nodules are clearly included, but the boundaries of other covered extraction are not.

10. **§ 2(1)—“Commercial” does not require commercial purpose.** The operative definition contains no sale, revenue, or profit requirement. Large-scale scientific recovery could therefore qualify, while profitable extraction below the numerical threshold might not, subject to the assessment exemption and risk-based provision.

11. **§ 2(1)(B)—Undefined “Secretary.”** The bill does not identify the official empowered to make comparable-risk determinations. Section 6 expressly names the Secretary of State, while section 4 assigns registry duties to NOAA, but neither clearly resolves this omission.

12. **§ 2(1)(B)—Indeterminate risk benchmark.** The bill supplies no criteria for comparing risks, including probability, severity, duration, spatial extent, or ecosystem sensitivity. Subparagraph (A) encompasses widely differing operations, leaving no single clear comparator.

13. **§ 2(1)(B)—Potentially unlimited activity scope.** “Any activity” is not expressly restricted to mining, mineral recovery, commercial conduct, or depths greater than 200 meters. A broad reading could capture unrelated activities with comparable ecosystem risks, creating substantial scope and fair-notice concerns.

14. **§ 2(1)(B)—Unspecified determination procedure and timing.** The bill does not say whether determinations must be made by rule, by order, or case by case, or when they become binding. Reliance on this provision to impose penalties for conduct preceding adequate notice would invite due-process challenges, especially criminally.

15. **§ 2(2)—Incomplete coverage of business entities.** The definition expressly covers only citizens and corporations organized under state law, not LLCs, partnerships, trusts, or other noncorporate entities. Those entities’ overseas activities are not clearly covered merely because they are U.S.-organized, although participating citizens may remain covered.

16. **§ 2(2)—D.C., territorial, and federally chartered corporations.** “State” is undefined, and corporations organized under District of Columbia, territorial, or federal law are not expressly included. Their status as U.S. persons is therefore uncertain.

17. **§ 2(2)—Noncitizen individuals abroad.** Lawful permanent residents and noncitizen U.S. nationals are not included merely by residence or nationality status. Their conduct outside the United States consequently falls outside the express citizenship-based jurisdictional rule.

18. **§§ 2(2), 3(a)—Foreign subsidiaries and attribution.** Foreign-organized corporations are not U.S. persons merely because Americans own or control them, and the bill supplies no ownership, control, or affiliate-attribution provision. This does not necessarily protect U.S. persons directing or participating in prohibited conduct, but ownership alone does not expressly bring the foreign entity within the definition.

19. **§ 3(a)—Undefined territorial reach.** “In the United States” does not specify treatment of territorial waters, the exclusive economic zone, the continental shelf, or U.S.-flagged vessels abroad. The express worldwide rule for U.S. persons does not resolve coverage of foreign persons in these settings.

20. **§ 3(a)—Unclear treatment of supporting activities.** “Engage in” is undefined, and the bill does not expressly prohibit financing, purchasing minerals, importing, transporting, or providing services to an otherwise prohibited operation. Some participation could still be reached through ordinary criminal complicity rules, but the bill establishes no comprehensive supply-chain prohibition.

### Exemptions

21. **§ 3(b)—Grandfathering without an expiration or transition limit.** The exemption has no independent end date, production cap, or phaseout requirement. Mining genuinely conducted under a qualifying exploration license could remain exempt while that license remains applicable.

22. **§ 3(b)—Unspecified licensing authority.** “Exploration license” is undefined and is not limited to a named U.S. agency or statutory licensing system. Whether foreign or international exploration authorizations qualify is consequently unresolved.

23. **§ 3(b)—Exploration license versus commercial mining.** The exemption applies to “mining conducted under an exploration license” without defining the permitted relationship between exploration and extraction. It could protect substantial licensed test recovery, but does not clearly excuse commercial production exceeding the license’s own authority.

24. **§ 3(b)—Renewals, amendments, transfers, and expansion.** The bill does not say whether a pre-enactment license retains grandfathered status after renewal, transfer, amendment, or expansion. It also lacks an express mechanism to prevent materially enlarged operations from claiming the original issuance date.

25. **§ 3(b)—No requirement that operations already exist.** Despite the heading “Existing Operations,” the operative text requires only a license issued before enactment. A license holder could therefore claim the exemption for qualifying operations begun later.

26. **§ 3(c)—Environmental-assessment exemption without substantive limits.** The exemption specifies no tonnage ceiling, duration, approval requirement, methodology, or independent oversight. Substantial recovery undertaken genuinely for environmental assessment could therefore be exempt.

27. **§ 3(c)—Mixed-purpose activities.** The text does not require environmental assessment to be the sole or primary purpose and does not address sale of recovered material. Activities combining assessment and commercial objectives present a significant interpretive gap, although simply labeling production an assessment would not necessarily suffice.

### Registry and reporting

28. **§§ 2(3), 4—Registry coverage does not match prohibited activity.** Vessels of exactly 5,000 gross tons or less are outside the registry requirement, even if they conduct prohibited mining. Conversely, a larger equipped vessel must apparently register even if inactive or engaged only in exempt activities; registration is not permission to mine.

29. **§ 2(3)—Undefined vessel and equipment boundaries.** The text does not specify the applicable gross-tonnage measurement system or when a vessel becomes “equipped” for recovery. Coverage of modular equipment, temporarily removed equipment, autonomous vehicles, and non-vessel platforms is consequently uncertain.

30. **§ 4(a)—Unspecified operator and geographic nexus.** “Operator” is undefined, leaving responsibility uncertain among owners, charterers, managers, and contractors. Unlike section 3, the registry provision also contains no express U.S.-person or territorial limitation, creating uncertainty about its intended application to foreign fleets.

31. **§ 4—Missing registration and reporting mechanics.** There is no initial registration deadline, quarterly filing deadline, prescribed reporting content beyond a description, or updating requirement. Section 4(b)’s reference to a “registered operator,” when section 4(a) requires registration of the vessel, adds uncertainty about who must report.

32. **§§ 4, 5—No express penalty for registry violations.** Section 5 penalizes violations of section 3, not failures to register or report under section 4. Other legal remedies or generally applicable false-statement laws might apply in appropriate circumstances, but this bill supplies no specific registry-enforcement penalty.

33. **§ 4(b)—Limited verification powers and data requirements.** Operator certification is required, but the bill provides no express audit, inspection, record-retention, or monitoring authority. It also does not expressly require tonnage, depth, location, or exemption information needed to test compliance.

### Enforcement and timing

34. **§§ 5(a), 8—Conflicting enactment and effective-date language.** Section 5(a) references violations occurring on or after enactment, while section 8 postpones the Act’s effectiveness for 180 days. Because section 3 ordinarily would not operate during that interval, the language creates avoidable uncertainty rather than clearly establishing enforceable interim liability.

35. **§ 8—Delayed commencement.** On the ordinary reading, the prohibition does not apply during the first 180 days after enactment. Operations during that period would remain subject to other applicable law, but not yet this prohibition.

36. **§ 5(a)—Unspecified civil enforcement process.** The bill identifies no civil enforcing agency, administrative assessment procedure, collection mechanism, or express injunction authority. Existing governmental and judicial authorities may fill some gaps, but the text leaves the enforcement architecture unresolved.

37. **§ 5(a)—Unclear unit of civil violation.** “For each day on which the violation occurs” does not establish whether separate vessels, projects, or acts generate separate daily penalties. That ambiguity materially affects maximum exposure for multi-vessel operations.

38. **§ 5(b)—Willfulness requirement against uncertain substantive rules.** Criminal liability requires a willful violation, but the bill does not define the required knowledge. Ambiguous thresholds, exemptions, and risk determinations could complicate proof and support fair-notice objections; they do not automatically defeat prosecution.

### International agreement and termination

39. **§ 6—Negotiation deadline without an outcome obligation.** “Shall seek to negotiate, not later than 18 months” is unclear about what milestone must occur by that date. It requires an effort, not a concluded agreement, and specifies neither counterparties nor minimum participation.

40. **§ 6—No implementation or foreign-competition solution.** The section does not itself bind foreign operators or supply domestic authority to implement a future agreement. “Equivalent” prohibitions is also undefined, including whether an agreement must reproduce section 3’s exemptions.

41. **§ 7(a)—Report prerequisite without a report mandate.** Termination depends on Congress acting on a National Academies report, but the bill neither commissions nor funds one, sets a deadline, nor specifies required findings. The contemplated early-termination mechanism could therefore lack its necessary evidentiary foundation.

42. **§ 7(a)—Undefined “without serious harm” standard.** The bill does not define seriousness, relevant harms, geographic scale, acceptable uncertainty, or whether the finding concerns particular technologies or the entire industry. This leaves the evidentiary standard for lifting the prohibition highly indeterminate.

43. **§ 7(a)—Joint-resolution procedure and termination scope.** The bill should specify an enacted joint resolution; ordinary constitutional requirements, including presentment, still apply. It also does not expressly say whether termination may be limited to particular activities or whether it necessarily lifts the entire section 3 prohibition.

44. **§ 7(a)—Registry survives early termination.** The early-termination provision ends the section 3 prohibition, not the entire Act. Registration and reporting duties therefore appear to continue until the ten-year sunset, even after Congress permits mining again.

45. **§ 7(b)—Unconditional sunset overrides the harm-based duration.** The entire Act expires ten years after enactment regardless of whether Congress has made the section 7(a) finding. Together with the delayed effective date, this produces an operative prohibition lasting approximately nine and a half years, not ten.

46. **§ 7(b)—No express transition or savings provisions.** The sunset does not address outstanding reports, pending proceedings, or previously incurred liabilities. The general federal saving statute, 1 U.S.C. § 109, may preserve penalties and liabilities, so expiration should not be treated as automatically erasing earlier violations.
